b:
When so many people are going hungry, should we travel, should we waste food, should we go for fine dining in restaurants, should we eat biryani when there's no way to get even a mouthful of rice, are lavish weddings really necessary, isn't plain khadi cloth enough….. you can stretch this on and on. Personally, I don't favour milk abhishekam in any form. In this modern age, milking itself is cruelty to animals. Every day, through milk packets, biscuits, paneer, curd, buttermilk, ghee, butter, in every way we share in the sin done to those animals that are injected with hormones, fed, made pregnant and kept shut in. But population growth and the economy make milk consumption essential

But wait, looking at this from the side of religion, it is certain that no god asks for milk to be poured by the cauldron. Even so, the dharma shastras speak of the merit of milk abhishekam.. My belief is that even if it's a single pot of milk, that devotion will bear fruit.

But in religions that have become commercialised, God is just an onlooker. This is the result of rituals becoming common property once a God who was confined to a particular group became universal. When the devotee sees his god cooled by a liquid he carried himself, from his own earnings, he too is cooled. He works hard, believing his business will thrive because of it. Not only that, the milk seller, the farmer, the man who set up a stall at this festival: everyone's economy grows from this single event.. And the milk poured over the copper idol goes out as prasadam. So it is not something you can dismiss entirely

We who ask why so much milk for a copper idol never stop to ask why flowers and food offerings for graves

Love

that's all it is
note: In an abhishekam, a temple idol is ritually bathed in milk and other offerings. Khadi is hand-spun cloth, a symbol of simplicity. The dharma shastras are Hindu texts on religious duty.
